questions.q: In YAML, how is nesting (like a dict inside a dict) represented?
questions.explain: YAML uses indentation (with spaces, never tabs) to represent nesting, instead of JSON's braces and brackets.

questions.q: Why should you use yaml.safe_load() instead of yaml.load()?
options: yaml.load() can be tricked by crafted input into constructing arbitrary Python objects, including ones that execute code
safe_load() supports comments while load() does not
There is no real difference between them
questions.explain: yaml.load() without a safe loader can instantiate arbitrary Python objects from specially crafted YAML, a real code-execution risk. safe_load() restricts parsing to plain data types.

questions.q: After calling yaml.safe_load() on a YAML mapping, what Python type do you get?
questions.explain: A YAML mapping becomes a Python dict, just like a JSON object does after json.load() — the same dict/list code works regardless of source format.

questions.q: Which of these is a genuine advantage YAML has over JSON for human-edited config files?
options: YAML is stricter about syntax than JSON
YAML requires curly braces for every object
questions.explain: YAML supports # comments, letting a person annotate a config file in place — something JSON's stricter syntax does not allow.

questions.q: Why would Northbridge's team choose INI over YAML for a particular settings file?
options: INI supports deeper nesting than YAML
INI is better for data exchanged between two programs
INI is the simplest option for flat key = value settings with no real nested structure
INI files can contain executable code safely
questions.explain: INI's [section] / key = value format is simplest for flat settings, but it can't represent nested structure well, which is why YAML or JSON is used for anything more complex.
